Certainly, if the ore was smelted in the same furnace the previous day, they heat up more quickly; if it was not smelted, they heat more slowly. If the hearth and the pit are not heated before the ore is cast in to be smelted, they will suffer damage, and the metals will suffer loss. For if the powder from which both are made is damp in the summer or frozen in the winter, both will burst and, sounding like a thunderclap together with the metals and other materials, scatter, not without great danger to the men. Then the master should cast slags into the furnace; these, once liquefied, will flow from the mouth into the pit. Soon he should block the mouth with clay, with which coal dust is mixed; he should apply this by hand to a round wooden pestle, five fingers thick and two spans high, whose handle is three feet long. Then, with a hooked iron bar, he should extract the slags from the pit, and if he is about to smelt ore rich in gold or silver, he should place a hundredweight of lead into it; if it is poor, half that amount. For the former requires much lead; the latter, little. Soon he should cast glowing firebrands onto the lead so that it liquefies. Afterward, he should perform all things rightly and cast them into the furnace in a certain order: first, such a portion of loaves made of <term>pyrites</term> <gloss>a metallic sulfur mineral</gloss> as is needed to smelt the ore; then, as much of the ore—mixed with silver foam, <term>molybdæna</term> <gloss>lead ore or litharge</gloss>, and stones that liquefy easily in fire of the second kind—as two troughs can hold; then, as many coals as a trough woven with wooden strips receives; finally, the slags. Once the furnace is filled with the aforementioned materials, he should smelt the ore gradually. But he should not pile it too much against the back wall of the furnace, lest it become fused near the nozzles of the bellows, impeding the air and causing the fire to burn less brightly. That man has certainly always been held in the number of excellent smelters who can temper the four elements. He tempers them who casts no more of the ore, which partakes of the earth, into the furnace than is appropriate; who pours in water as often as the situation demands; who moderates the blast of the bellows with skill; and who casts the ore into the fire at the part where it burns brightly. The master indeed, by pouring water little by little into both sides of the furnace, should dampen the coals so that the thinnest particles of the ores adhere to them, which would otherwise be agitated by the blast of the bellows and the force of the fires, lifted up, and fly away with the smoke. But because the nature of the ores to be smelted is diverse, it is necessary for smelters to prepare the hearth now high and now low, and to place the pipe in which the nozzles of the bellows are situated sometimes very sloped and sometimes only slightly; and to breathe into the furnace a blast of the bellows now gentle and now vehement. For ores that heat and liquefy quickly, smelters need a low hearth, a pipe placed with little slope, and a gentle blast of the bellows; on the contrary, for those that heat and liquefy slowly, they need a high hearth, a pipe placed with much slope, and a vehement blast of the bellows. For these, they also need a furnace that is well-heated and in which slags, or loaves made of pyrites, or stones that liquefy easily in fire have been cooked beforehand. If these things are not done, the ores sitting in the hearth of the furnace block the mouth and as it were suffocate it, which also happens when small metallic particles, which settled while the ores were being washed, are used. Moreover, the large bellows should have wide nozzles; for if they are narrow, a great and powerful blast is breathed into the furnace too tightly and sharply, from which the liquefied material is cooled and becomes fused around the nozzles,
